Don't rely on mysqli_real_escape_string. The preferred method is to create prepared statements.

Once you go prepared or stored queries you will never go back. The security level is a whole jump above sending full query strings formed in your PHP or elsewhere.

I prefer stored functions/procedures. You write them directly into your mysql DB and only pass the variables when requested. Say I have a query for news like:


 SELECT * from `newsArticles` Where `rating` > 3 AND `author` = 'Rosso'

This could be writen as stored procedure with name for example "newsGrab" and then when called in PHP through mysqli your statement string is

CALL newsGrab(3, 'Rosso')

. If you combine that with a prepared statement then you are winning. Injection attacks have solid prevention now.

$statement = $mysqliConnection->prepare(CALL newsGrab(?, ?));

$statement = $statement->bind_param("is", $startRatingInt, $authorStr);

note first parameter of @bind_param "is" tells the function expect parameters after to be an int (i) followed by string (s)

In humans, retrospective studies support the conclusion that NSAID therapy can impair fracture healing. In perhaps the most compelling retrospective study, Burd et al. (14) examined data collected from a randomized, prospective trial to compare localized radiation therapy to indomethacin (a nonselective NSAID) therapy on the incidence and severity of heterotopic ossification after hip fracture surgery to determine whether NSAID therapy affects fracture healing. Heterotopic ossification is the formation of bone at sites outside of the normal skeleton and occurs through a mixture of intramembranous and endochondral ossification (6, 51, 64). Heterotopic ossification commonly occurs following hip fractures and can reduce hip mobility depending upon the extent of bone formation. To prevent heterotopic ossification after hip fracture surgery, patients are treated with localized radiation or with a 6-wk course of NSAID therapy (64, 95). Burd et al. (15) performed a randomized, prospective study to determine whether localized radiation or NSAID therapy was more effective at reducing heterotopic ossification after hip fractures (15). The study found that localized radiation or 6 wk of postoperative NSAID treatment both effectively reduced heterotopic ossification. However, many of the patients in this study also suffered additional long bone fractures coincident with their hip fractures. When the healing outcomes for those patients who suffered additional long bone fractures were compared between those who received localized radiation or no heterotopic ossification prophylaxis (74 patients) versus those that received indomethacin therapy (38 patients), 29% of the indomethacin-treated patients developed a nonunion while only 7% of patients that did not receive indomethacin developed a nonunion (14). Further, 11 of the 72 long bone fractures in the 38 indomethacin-treated patients developed nonunions while only 5 of the 118 long bone fractures in the comparator group of 74 patients developed nonunions. These data were statistically significant and clearly indicate that NSAID therapy is detrimental for fracture healing. Other retrospective studies support this conclusion (25, 44). In addition, NSAIDs inhibit heterotopic bone formation, which often develops through an endochondral ossification mechanism (71, 81). Thus it is not necessarily surprising that bone healing which requires endochondral ossification would be inhibited by NSAID treatment.

It's a little more complicated than that. I joke about the idiots who say they are allergic to acetaminophen but can take norco, but there are a lot of other enmeshed issues. Currently the US is about 5% of the world population, yet we consume 80% of the global supply of opioids. We have a problem.

There are several contributing issues. Firstly, Americans don't deal well with pain. For many people, the only acceptable level of pain is zero, which is horseshit. I get very frequent kidney stones (from the shallow end of the gene pool) and I generally treat then with non-narcotic medications. Maybe 10% I'll take a Norco or two. But I also am shooting for a 4/10 level of pain. That's a reasonable expectation, but it's not enough for some.

Secondly, some Americans are highly risk averse when it comes to medicines and they want to avoid taking meds - even if that is more dangerous for them. This is the guy who gets a stoke from untreated hypertension because he doesn't want to be a "pill taker". There is also a moralistic bullshit that people should be able to keep themselves healthy and not take meds with willpower alone. If you have to take pills, you are weak.

So these all combine not infrequently in patients who only want to take medicines that they feel are helpful for them (i.e. that manages a symptom they don't like). It's not just with pain either... it's the asthmatic who doesn't want to take the inhaled steroids to prevent the use of their rescue inhaler because they don't feel better right after the preventative med as they do when they take a hit of albuterol. Unfortunately, if they took the steroid inhaler regularly in many cases would never or rarely need the albuterol and their risk of hospitalization and death is decreased significantly. In pain patients this is the guy with a bad back who only wants to take opioid pain meds. Prescribe anything else, refer him to someone for treatment, and he googles it and sees any scary sounding side effect and refuses it, despite the fact that the oxycodone he wants is a metric fuckton more dangerous. However, the risk-averse attitude is not applied to patient desired medications.

Every year about 16,000 people die from prescription opioids in the US. Acetaminophen kills less than 500. The numbers are even more staggering when you compare them per use, since acetaminophen is used far more extensively in the US than opioids. Moreover unlike opioids, the majority of the deaths from acetaminophen are intentional. With NSAIDs, about 3,500 people die each year in the US from these medicines - so less than 1/4 as opioids. Again per use the data show even greater safety for NSAIDs compared with opioids - since they are more often used. This is the FDA's take on the numbers.

As far as opioid seekers spreading this disinformation, it's not that Machiavellian. I think a lot of it is self-justifying their behaviors. Knowing the greater safety of acetaminophen/NSAIDs compared with opioids (which almost all of them have heard from at least one doctor) creates a cognitive dissonance that they must try to fix. Their 'internet advocacy' to show how evil acetaminophen/NSAIDs are helps them to deal with that dissonance. It's like people who are creationists, or think the moon landing was faked - if you're supporting a bullshit idea to maintain some inner sense of yourself being a good/smart/health concious person (i.e. not a 'sheeple', etc) you have to blow a lot of bullshit out of your ass.
